questions.question_text: For the function $f(x) = \dfrac{8}{x}$, which statement correctly describes its behaviour as $x \to \infty$ and as $x \to 0^+$?

options.why: Assumed $k < 0$, reversing the sign of $y$ for positive $x$ values.
Swapped the horizontal asymptote limit as $x \to \infty$ with the vertical asymptote limit as $x \to 0^+$.
Substituted $x = 1$ into the numerator instead of evaluating the limit as $x \to 0^+$.

questions.solution_text:
For $f(x) = \dfrac{8}{x}$ with $k = 8 > 0$:
As $x \to \infty$, $x > 0$ becomes arbitrarily large, so $y = \dfrac{8}{x} > 0$ approaches $0$ from above.
As $x \to 0^+$, $x > 0$ is small and positive, so $y = \dfrac{8}{x} \to \infty$.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the end behaviour of $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x}$ as $x \to \infty$ and as $x \to -\infty$?

options.text: As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from above; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from below.
As $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ from below; as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.
options.why: Reversed the signs of $y$ in the first and third quadrants.
Confused the end behaviour with a linear or cubic polynomial function.
Assumed the horizontal limit approaches the numerator $k$ rather than zero.

questions.solution_text:
Since $k = 5 > 0$:
When $x$ is large and positive, $y = \dfrac{5}{x} > 0$ and approaches $0$, so $y \to 0$ from above.
When $x$ is large and negative, $y = \dfrac{5}{x} < 0$ and approaches $0$, so $y \to 0$ from below.

questions.question_text: For the function $f(x) = -\dfrac{2}{x}$, what is the behaviour of $y$ as $x$ approaches $0$ from the positive side ($x \to 0^+$)?

options.why: Ignored the negative sign in the numerator $-2$, assuming $y \to \infty$ as for $k > 0$.
Confused the vertical asymptote behaviour at $x = 0$ with the end behaviour as $x \to \infty$.
Substituted $x = 1$ into the numerator instead of taking the limit as $x \to 0^+$.

questions.solution_text:
As $x \to 0^+$, $x$ is small and positive, so $\dfrac{2}{x} \to \infty$.
With the negative sign, $y = -\dfrac{2}{x} \to -\infty$.

options.text: $C_1$ lies further from both coordinate axes than $C_2$ for all $x \neq 0$.
$C_1$ lies closer to both coordinate axes than $C_2$ for all $x \neq 0$.
options.why: Assumed the outer curve $C_1$ is compressed closer to the axes rather than expanded outward.

options.text: $C_1$ and $C_2$ have different vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
options.why: Believed that different dilation constants change the asymptotes from $x = 0$ and $y = 0$.

options.text: $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect each other at very large values of $x$.
options.why: Believed that the two hyperbolas eventually intersect as they both approach the horizontal asymptote.

questions.solution_text:
Both curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ are hyperbolas lying in Quadrants $1$ and $3$ with asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = 0$.
Curve $C_1$ is dilated outward compared to $C_2$, so $C_1$ lies further from both coordinate axes for all $x \neq 0$.

questions.question_text: A hyperbola $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ passes through the point $(3, -5)$. What are its quadrants and end behaviour as $x \to \infty$?

options.why: Assumed $k > 0$ without calculating $k = 3 \times (-5) = -15$.
Treated the $y$-coordinate of the given point as the horizontal asymptote.
Named adjacent quadrants $1$ and $4$ instead of opposite quadrants $2$ and $4$.

questions.solution_text:
$k = x \times y = 3 \times (-5) = -15$.
Since $k < 0$, the branches lie in Quadrants $2$ and $4$.
As $x \to \infty$, $y = -\dfrac{15}{x} < 0$, so $y \to 0$ from below.

questions.question_text: In which quadrants does the graph of $f(x) = -\dfrac{9}{x}$ lie, and what are its asymptotes?

options.why: Assumed every hyperbola lies in quadrants $1$ and $3$, ignoring the sign of $k$.
Took the numerator $-9$ as the vertical asymptote instead of reading it from $x = 0$.
Ignored the sign of $k$ when placing the branches and also read $-9$ as the vertical asymptote.

questions.solution_text:
For $f(x) = -\dfrac{9}{x}$, $k = -9 < 0$.
The branches occupy Quadrants $2$ and $4$, and the asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = 0$.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = -\dfrac{10}{x}$, which statement correctly describes its behaviour as $x \to -\infty$ and as $x \to 0^-$?

options.why: Reversed the signs of $y$, which are positive for all $x < 0$ when $k = -10$.
Swapped the horizontal limit with the vertical asymptote limit.
Incorrectly claimed $y \to -\infty$ as $x \to 0^-$ despite $-10/x > 0$ for $x < 0$.

questions.question_text: A function $f(x) = \dfrac{k}{x}$ has the property that as $x \to 0^+$, $y \to -\infty$, and passes through $(5, -1)$. What is the equation of $f(x)$ and its behaviour as $x \to -\infty$?

options.why: Calculated $k = 5$ instead of $k = 5 \times (-1) = -5$.
Gave an infinite limit for end behaviour instead of the horizontal asymptote $y \to 0$.
Divided the coordinates as $y/x = -1/5$ instead of multiplying $k = xy = -5$.

questions.solution_text:
$k = xy = 5 \times (-1) = -5$, so $f(x) = -\dfrac{5}{x}$.
Since $k = -5 < 0$, for $x < 0$ we have $y > 0$, so as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to 0$ from above.

questions.question_text: Consider the curves $C_1: y = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $C_2: y = -\dfrac{8}{x}$. Which statement is true regarding their distances from the origin and their asymptotes?

options.text: Both curves have the same asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = 0$, and $C_2$ is further from the origin at corresponding $|x|$ values than $C_1$.
$C_2$ has different asymptotes than $C_1$ because its constant is negative.
options.why: Believed a negative constant shifts or rotates the asymptote lines.

options.text: $C_1$ is further from the origin because $3$ is positive while $-8$ is negative.
options.why: Compared signed values $3 > -8$ rather than the absolute magnitudes $|-8| > 3$.

options.text: Both curves have identical distance from the origin at all points.
options.why: Ignored the difference in dilation factors between $k = 3$ and $k = -8$.

questions.solution_text:
All reciprocal functions $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$ share asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = 0$.
The distance from the axes depends on $|k|$; since $|-8| = 8 > 3$, $C_2$ is further from the origin than $C_1$.
